title: Immune Neglect
text:
In 1998 Daniel Gilbert, Elizabeth Pinel, Timothy Wilson, Stephen Blumberg and Thalia Wheatley published a series of studies on how well people predict their own emotional reactions to bad news.

In one study, they surveyed assistant professors at a large university about how happy they expected to be in the years after a tenure decision went for or against them. They also surveyed former assistant professors who had already been granted or denied tenure. The junior faculty expected to be considerably less happy for years if they were denied. But those who had actually been turned down were, on average, about as happy as those who had succeeded.

Similar gaps appeared elsewhere. Students predicted how they would feel some months after a romantic relationship ended, and those whose relationships had in fact ended were happier than predicted. Voters in a Texas governor's race expected their candidate's defeat to bother them for a month; a month later it bothered them much less than they had forecast. In a lab study, people rejected for a job by a single evaluator recovered faster than they expected.

The researchers called this immune neglect. People have a psychological immune system: they find silver linings, reinterpret events and move on. But they do not take this ability into account when they imagine the future, so they overestimate how long setbacks will hurt.
lesson: When you fear a setback, remember that you will likely adapt and recover faster than you now imagine. Do not let an exaggerated fear of disappointment keep you from trying.
people: Daniel Gilbert, Elizabeth Pinel, Timothy Wilson, Stephen Blumberg, Thalia Wheatley
location: University of Texas at Austin and other US universities, USA
source: Gilbert, D. T., Pinel, E. C., Wilson, T. D., Blumberg, S. J., and Wheatley, T. P. (1998). Immune neglect: A source of durability bias in affective forecasting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(3), 617-638.
